A right-angled triangle has $\tan\theta=\dfrac{5}{12}$.
Every side is multiplied by $6$.
What is $\tan\theta$ in the new triangle?

questions.question_text: Which of these is **impossible** for an angle $\theta$ in a right-angled triangle?

options.why: The opposite side may be longer than the adjacent side, so a tangent ratio above $1$ is possible.
The adjacent side may be almost as long as the hypotenuse, so a cosine close to $1$ is possible.
The opposite side may be slightly shorter than the adjacent side, so a tangent just below $1$ is possible.

questions.question_text: Why is it impossible for an angle $\theta$ in a right-angled triangle to have $\cos\theta=0$?

options.text: The adjacent side would have length $0$, so there would be no triangle.

options.why: Confuses the numerator with the denominator: a zero cosine ratio would require the adjacent side, not the hypotenuse, to be zero.

options.text: The adjacent side would equal the hypotenuse.
options.why: Confuses a cosine ratio of $0$ with a ratio of $1$, which would make these two lengths equal.

options.text: The opposite side would have length $0$.
options.why: Uses the sine ratio instead of the cosine ratio; cosine compares the adjacent side with the hypotenuse.

questions.solution_text:
$\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{Adj}}{\text{Hyp}}=0$ would require $\text{Adj}=0$.
A side of a triangle cannot have zero length, so such a right-angled triangle is impossible.
